overview:
Guinea curves like a crescent along the Atlantic coast of West Africa, bordered by Guinea-Bissau, Senegal, Mali, Ivory Coast, Liberia, and Sierra Leone. It is about the size of Oregon. The capital, Conakry, spreads along a narrow peninsula and islands jutting into the sea, so the city is long and thin and always close to the water. Guinea is sometimes called Guinea-Conakry to avoid confusion with Guinea-Bissau and Equatorial Guinea.

About 14 million people live in Guinea, and French is the official language, though Fula, Malinke, and Susu are the languages of home and market. Nearly 90 percent of Guineans are Muslim. Guinea holds the world's largest reserves of bauxite, the ore used to make aluminum, along with iron, gold, and diamonds, yet most people remain poor and farm rice, cassava, and bananas. The country is a republic that has experienced several military takeovers, most recently in 2021. Its rivers feed much of West Africa, and its musicians and dancers have influenced the entire region.
landAndNature: Four regions make up Guinea. The coastal lowland is hot, humid, and laced with mangrove estuaries. Behind it rises the Fouta Djallon, a highland of sandstone plateaus, waterfalls, and deep valleys where cool air and heavy rain give birth to three of West Africa's great rivers, the Niger, Senegal, and Gambia, which is why Guinea is called the water tower of the region. Upper Guinea to the east is dry savanna along the upper Niger, and the forested Guinea Highlands in the southeast rise to Mount Nimba, 1,752 meters, whose slopes shelter chimpanzees that use stone tools and a rare toad that gives birth to live young. Hippos live in the rivers, and the coast is a stopover for millions of migrating birds.
peopleAndCulture: The Fula, or Peul, dominate the Fouta Djallon as cattle herders and traders, the Malinke live in the east, and the Susu along the coast; each has its own language, music, and dress. Meals are built on rice with sauces of peanut, palm oil, or leaf greens, and fish or meat, along with fried plantains and mangoes in season. Guinea's music is legendary: the balafon, the kora harp, and above all the djembe drum, whose players from Guinea taught the instrument to the world. Les Ballets Africains, the national dance company, has toured for decades, and singer Mory Kanté made international hits. Soccer is the favorite sport, and Guinean tailors are known across the region for embroidered robes called boubous.
history: The region was part of the great Mali Empire in the 1200s and 1300s, and in the 1700s Fula Muslim leaders founded a powerful state in the Fouta Djallon. Samori Touré built the Wassoulou Empire in the late 1800s and fought French troops for years before his capture in 1898. France ruled Guinea as a colony until 1958, when Guineans voted no in a referendum on staying with France, and became independent on October 2, 1958, the first French colony in Africa to do so. The first president, Ahmed Sékou Touré, ruled harshly until his death in 1984. Military leader Lansana Conté then governed until 2008. Guinea held its first truly democratic election in 2010, but the army seized power again in 2021.
funFacts: Three great rivers, the Niger, Senegal, and Gambia, all begin in Guinea's Fouta Djallon highlands.
Guinea holds roughly a quarter of the world's known bauxite, the ore used to make aluminum for cans and airplanes.
The Mount Nimba toad is one of the only toads in the world that gives birth to live babies instead of laying eggs.
Chimpanzees at Bossou in Guinea crack nuts with stone hammers and anvils, a skill studied by scientists for decades.
Conakry's main island, Tombo, is linked to the mainland by a causeway, and the city stretches 36 kilometers along a peninsula.
